q: Where is Ilocano mainly spoken, and how big is it?
a: Northern Luzon: the Ilocos provinces, La Union, Abra and much of the Cagayan Valley. It's the **third most spoken native language** of the Philippines (about 8–9 million first-language speakers) and the lingua franca of the Cordillera.
hint: North of Manila, and more than one region.

q: Is Ilocano a dialect of Tagalog?
a: No. They're **related but separate languages**: a Tagalog speaker can't follow an Ilocano conversation. The grammar machinery (predicate first, markers, focus) is similar, which helps a lot.
hint: Related is not the same as mutually intelligible.

q: What is 'Samtoy'?
a: An old name Ilocanos use for their language, from **sao mi ditoy**, "our language here".

q: How do you pronounce doubled consonants like the pp in **uppat** (four)?
a: **Hold them**: *oop-pat*, like the k-k in "book-case". Doubling changes meaning: **anak** (a child) vs **annak** (children).

q: What does a hyphen inside a word like **nalam-ek** (cold) tell you?
a: It marks a **glottal stop**: the catch in "uh-oh". Say *nalam* + catch + *ek*.

q: Why is the letter **e** tricky in Ilocano?
a: In native words many speakers (especially outside the Ilocos provinces) say it as a central vowel English lacks; in the Ilocos and in Spanish loans it's a plain *e* as in "bet". Copy the speakers around you.
hint: It depends on region and on whether the word is a loan.

q: What's the default word order of an Ilocano sentence?
a: **Predicate first, subject last**, with no verb "to be": **Napintas ni Ana** = beautiful / Ana = "Ana is beautiful."

q: How do you ask "How are you?" to one person, and to an elder or a group?
a: **Kumustaka?** to one person; **Kumustakayo?** to several people or politely to one older person.

q: Give a natural reply to **Kumustaka?**
a: **Naimbag met, agyamanak. Sika?** or **Mayat met, agyamanak. Sika?** — "I'm fine too, thanks. And you?"

q: Say "Good morning", "Good afternoon" and "Good evening".
a: **Naimbag a bigat**, **Naimbag a malem**, **Naimbag a rabii**. (And **Naimbag nga aldaw** = good day.)

q: How do you say "Thank you" in Ilocano, and what's the heartfelt version?
a: **Agyamanak** (also spelled *agyamannak*); **Agyamanak unay** = thank you very much. **Dios ti agngina** ("God will repay you") is the deep, heartfelt thanks.

q: What do **Wen** and **Saan** mean?
a: **Wen** = yes. **Saan** (spoken **Haan**) = **no**.

q: Ask someone's name, and give yours.
a: **Ania ti naganmo?** → **Siak ni ___.** or **Ti naganko ket ___.**

q: How do you say "I'm from Vigan"?
a: **Taga-Vigan ak.** (Ask: **Taga-anoka?** — "Where are you from?")

q: What does **Innakon** mean, and when do you say it?
a: "I'm going now." A common goodbye. (**Inkamin** = we're going now.) The **-n** means "now, already".

q: How do you say "Excuse me" (to get attention) and "I'm sorry"?
a: **Pakawanennak** (excuse me / forgive me) and **Dispensarennak** (I'm sorry).

q: What are the **-ak set** endings (the one the sentence is about)?
a: **-ak** I · **-ka** you · *(nothing)* he/she · **-ta** we two · **-tayo** we all · **-kami** we (not you) · **-kayo** you all/polite · **-da** they.

q: What is the -ak-set ending for "he/she"?
a: **Nothing at all.** **Nabannog** alone means "He/she is tired". Context tells you who.

q: What's the difference between **-ta**, **-tayo** and **-kami** ("we")?
a: **-ta** = you and me only; **-tayo** = all of us including you; **-kami** = us but **not** you.

q: Why is "my spouse" **asawak** but "my house" **balayko**?
a: **-ko** and **-mo** shrink to **-k** and **-m** after a vowel (*asawa* ends in a vowel); after a consonant they stay whole (*balay*).
hint: Look at the last letter of the noun.

q: Give the stand-alone pronouns for I, you, he/she and they.
a: **siak**, **sika**, **isu / isuna**, **isuda**. (Also **dakami**, **datayo**, **data**, **dakayo**.)
hint: Used when the pronoun is the whole answer.

q: Where does a pronoun ending attach in a sentence?
a: To the **first word**, whatever it is: **Napanak** (I went) but **Saanak a napan** (I didn't go): the -ak jumped onto *saan*.

q: What do **kaniak** and **kenka** mean?
a: "To/for me" and "to/for you", the oblique forms. **Itedmo kaniak** = Give it to me.

q: Break down **Ay-ayatenka** (I love you).
a: **ayaten** (love someone, -en focus) in the ongoing form **ay-ayaten** + **-ka**, a fused "I → you" ending.

q: Which marker does the jobs of both Tagalog *ang* and *ng*?
a: **ti** (plural **dagiti**). It marks the subject, the owner and the doer; **word order and the verb** tell them apart.

q: What does **iti** mark?
a: The **oblique**: place, direction, recipient (**iti eskuelaan** = to the school) and an **indefinite object** (**Nangan iti saba** = He ate a banana).

q: What's the difference between **ti saba** and **iti saba** after an actor-focus verb?
a: **ti saba** = *the* banana (definite); **iti saba** = *a* banana (indefinite).

q: Which markers go in front of a person's name?
a: **ni** in the core (**Napintas ni Ana**) and **ken ni** in the oblique (**Itedmo ken ni Ben**). Plurals: **da** / **kada**.

q: Say "the teacher's house".
a: **ti balay ti maestra**: the owner takes **ti**, like English "of".

q: What do **ken**, **ket**, **ngem** and **wenno** mean?
a: **ken** = and (between nouns), **ket** = and (between clauses, also links a topic), **ngem** = but / than, **wenno** = or.

q: How can Ilocano make a noun plural without **dagiti**?
a: By **doubling a sound** in the noun: **ubing → ubbing** (children), **lalaki → lallaki** (men), **anak → annak**.

q: What are the three words for "this/that"?
a: **daytoy** (near me), **dayta** (near **you**, the listener), **daydiay** (far from both).

q: Your friend is holding a plate. Do you ask **Ania daytoy?** or **Ania dayta?**
a: **Ania dayta?**: **dayta** is "that, near you", anchored to the listener.

q: What do **ditoy**, **dita** and **idiay** mean?
a: here, there (by you), over there. **idiay** also means "to/in" a named or far place: **idiay Vigan**.

q: How do you say "Do you have a car?"
a: **Adda kadi kotsem?**: **adda** (there is) + **kotse** + **-m** (your). There's no verb "to have".

q: How do you say "There's no coffee", and why not use **saan**?
a: **Awan ti kape.** **awan** denies existence or having; **saan** negates verbs, adjectives and identities.

q: Ask "Where's the bathroom?"
a: **Ayanna ti banio?** (or the shorter **Ayan ti banio?**): **ayan** = location.

q: What does **Addadtoyak!** mean, and when do you say it?
a: "I'm here!": what you call out on arriving at someone's house. (**adda** + **ditoy** + **-ak**)

q: How do you say "mine" and "yours"?
a: **kukuak** and **kukuam** (*kukua* = property + owner ending). **kukuana** = his/hers.

q: What prefix do most Ilocano adjectives start with?
a: **na-**: **napintas** (beautiful), **naimas** (delicious), **nalaing** (clever), **napudot** (hot). Exceptions include **dakkel** (big) and **bassit** (small).

q: Why is it **naimbag nga aldaw** but **naimbag a bigat**?
a: Working rule for the linker: **nga before a vowel** (*aldaw*), **a before a consonant** (*bigat*).
hint: Look at the next word's first letter.

q: Say "a beautiful house" two ways. Does the meaning change?
a: **napintas a balay** = **balay a napintas**. The words can swap places with the same linker **a** in the middle, and the meaning stays the same. Adjective-first is more common in speech.
hint: The linker sits between the two words, whichever comes first.

q: Say "two houses", "three children" and "this house". What joins each pair?
a: **dua a balay** · **tallo nga ubbing** · **daytoy a balay**. Numbers and demonstratives join their noun with the same linker as adjectives: **a** before a consonant, **nga** before a vowel (*ubbing* starts with a vowel).
hint: The same a / nga glue from lesson 6.

q: How do you say "very delicious" and "so delicious!"?
a: **Naimas unay** (very) and **Nagimasen!** (*nag- + root + -en*: an exclamation).

q: How do you form "the most ___"?
a: **ka- + root + -an**: **ti kaimasan** (the most delicious), **ti kapudotan** (the hottest).

q: Say "I'm tired".
a: **Nabannogak.**: the adjective **nabannog** + **-ak**. The adjective is the whole predicate.

q: What are the main actor-focus verb affixes?
a: **ag-** (agbasa, read), **-um-** (gumatang, buy), **mang-** (mangan, eat), and **ma-** for a few verbs (maturog, sleep; mapan, go).

q: How do you make the **completed** form of ag-, mang- and ma- verbs?
a: Swap **m** for **n**: **ag- → nag-** (nagbasa), **mang- → nang-** (nangan), **ma- → na-** (napan, naturog).

q: What's the completed form of an **-um-** verb?
a: **-um-** becomes **-imm-**: **gumatang → gimmatang** (bought), **umay → immay** (came), **uminom → imminom** (drank).

q: How do you make the **ongoing** form ("is doing")?
a: **Double the first syllable of the root**: **agbasa → agbasbasa**, **gumatang → gumatgatang**, **agadal → agad-adal**.

q: How is the future shown in Ilocano?
a: There's no future form: use the **neutral verb + pronoun + -to** (**-nto** after a vowel): **Mapanakto** (I'll go), **Agawidkayonto** (you'll go home).

q: How do you say "Let's eat!"
a: **Mangantayo!** (or **Mangantayon!**, "let's eat now"). Neutral verb + **-tayo**.

q: What does **Nanganka?** mean, and how do you answer?
a: "Have you eaten?": a greeting as much as a question. Answer **Wen, nanganakon** ("Yes, I've eaten already").

q: What's the feel difference between **ag-** and **-um-** on the same root?
a: **ag-** = repeated, lasting or deliberate; **-um-** = a single action or a change. **agtakder** (be standing) vs **tumakder** (stand up).

q: What do the focus affixes **-en**, **i-** and **-an** focus on?
a: **-en**: the thing affected (basaen, read it); **i-**: the thing given/put/said (ited, give it); **-an**: the person or place targeted (suratan, write to someone).

q: What's the difference between **Nagbasaak iti libro** and **Binasak ti libro**?
a: Same event. The first focuses on **me** and the book is indefinite (*a* book); the second focuses on **the book** (definite), with me as the doer in the -ko set.

q: How do you form the completed form of an **-en** verb?
a: Infix **-in-** and drop **-en**: **basaen → binasa**, **gatangen → ginatang**, **aramiden → inaramid**.

q: What happens when **-en** meets **-ko** or **-mo**?
a: They fuse: **-en + ko → -ek**, **-en + mo → -em**. **Ania ti aramidem?** = What are you doing?

q: In **Dinalusak ti sala** (I cleaned the living room), what is the **-ak**?
a: Not the -ak "I" set: it's **-an + -ko** fused ("by me"). **-an + mo → -am**.

q: How do you say "Give it to me" and "Help me"?
a: **Itedmo kaniak.** (i- verb *ited*) and **Tulongannak.** (*tulongan* + fused "you → me").

q: What's the completed form of **ited** (give) and **ibaga** (say)?
a: **inted** and **imbaga**: **i- → in-**, usually **im-** before *b/p*.

q: Say "I want coffee" and "I need help".
a: **Kayatko ti kape.** and **Masapulko ti tulong.**: the wanter takes the **-ko** set.

q: How do you say "I don't know"?
a: **Diak ammo.**: **di** + **-k**. Never *diko*.

q: What does **maka-** do to a verb?
a: Makes it "be able to": **makaturog** (be able to sleep), **makasao** (be able to speak). Completed: **naka-**.

q: Ask "Do you speak Ilocano?" and reply "Just a little".
a: **Agsasaoka iti Ilokano?** → **Bassit laeng.** (*agsasao* is the ongoing form of *agsao*, speak.)

q: Say "I don't understand" two ways.
a: **Saanko a maawatan.** or **Diak maawatan.**

q: What's the difference between **saan** and **di** as negatives?
a: **saan** (or *haan*) needs a linker: **Saanak a napan**. **di** doesn't: **Diak napan**. Both mean "I didn't go".

q: How do you make a negative command ("don't …")?
a: Put the pronoun on **di**: **Dika mapan** (Don't go), **Dikayo…** to several people. With a 'me' in it: **Dinak ig-igaman** (Don't touch me).

q: What do **Saan pay** and **Awan ti problema** mean?
a: "Not yet" and "No problem".

q: How do you politely refuse more food?
a: **Nanganakon, agyamanak.** ("I've already eaten, thanks"), or **Bassit laeng, apo** ("just a little") if refusing outright would be rude.

q: What does the ending **-n** (*-en*, *-on*) add, as in **Nanganakon**?
a: "**Already / now**": **Nanganakon** = I've eaten already; **Mapantayon** = let's go now.

q: What does **kadi** do?
a: Marks a **yes/no question**, like Tagalog *ba*: **Adda kadi kape?** = Is there coffee?

q: What does **man** do in **Itedmo man kaniak**?
a: **Softens a request**: "Could you give it to me?" instead of a flat command.

q: What do **gayam**, **kano** and **ngata** mean?
a: **gayam** = so it turns out (*pala*); **kano** = reportedly (*daw*); **ngata** = maybe/probably (*yata*).

q: What do **ngamin** and **ngarud** mean?
a: **ngamin** = because, you see (gives a reason); **ngarud** = so, then, indeed (**Wen ngarud!** = Yes, of course!).

q: What do **met**, **laeng** and **pay** mean?
a: **met** = too/also, and a softener; **laeng** = only, just; **pay** = still, yet, more (**Maysa pay** = one more).

q: Where do particles go in the sentence?
a: **After the first word and its pronoun ending**: **Nabannogak met.** · **Nanganka kadin?**

q: Give the Ilocano for what, who, where (to), when, why, how, how much.
a: **Ania**, **Siasino**, **Sadino**, **Kaano**, **Apay**, **Kasano**, **Mano**. (**Ayan** = where something is.)

q: What does **Papanam?** mean, and how do you answer?
a: "Where are you going?": a friendly check-in. Answer lightly: **Idiay tiendaan** (to the market) or **Idiay laeng** (just over there).

q: How do you ask "When?" about the past vs the future?
a: **Idi kaano?** (past) vs **Inton kaano?** (future).

q: What's **Aniat' naganmo?**
a: A spoken contraction of **Ania ti naganmo?**: "What's your name?"

q: Count 1–5 in Ilocano.
a: **maysa, dua, tallo, uppat, lima.**

q: Count 6–10 in Ilocano.
a: **innem, pito, walo, siam, sangapulo.**

q: How do you say 20, 100 and 1,000?
a: **duapulo**, **sangagasut**, **sangaribu**. (**sanga-** = one, before a unit.)
hint: two tens, one hundred, one thousand.

q: Which number system do Ilocanos use to tell the time?
a: **Spanish**: **alas tres** (3 o'clock), **alas siete y medya** (7:30). *Tallo nga oras* would mean "three hours".

q: Say "yesterday", "now/today" and "tomorrow".
a: **idi kalman**, **ita**, **intono bigat**.

q: Ask "How much is this?" and react "That's expensive!"
a: **Mano daytoy?** → **Nangina met!** (Then: **Adda kadi nalaklaka?** = Is there a cheaper one?)

q: What is **apo** used for?
a: **Respect**, like Tagalog *po*: **Wen, apo**, **Agyamanak, apo**. It also means **grandchild**, and is a title of honour (**Apo Dios**).

q: How else do you show respect to one older person?
a: Use the **plural kayo** instead of ka: **Kumustakayo, apo?** (a T-V distinction, like *usted*).

q: What do **manong**, **manang** and **ading** mean?
a: Older brother/any older man, older sister/any older woman, younger sibling/anyone younger. Used warmly with strangers too.

q: What do **kabsat**, **uliteg**, **ikit** and **kasinsin** mean?
a: sibling, uncle, aunt, cousin.

q: Name three Ilocano dishes.
a: **pinakbet** (vegetables with bagoong), **dinengdeng** (vegetable broth), **bagnet** (crispy pork), also **Vigan longganisa**, **empanada**, and **basi** (sugarcane wine).

q: What are the Ilocano meanings of **bigat**, **sabong** and **mano**?
a: **bigat** = morning (not 'heavy'), **sabong** = flower (not 'cockfight'), **mano** = how much/many (not the blessing gesture).

q: What is **Biag ni Lam-ang**?
a: "The Life of Lam-ang": the Ilocano epic, whose hero talks at birth and is brought back to life by his rooster and dog.

q: How do you say "bigger", "cheaper" and "Their house is bigger than ours"?
a: Double the root's first syllable: **dakdakkel** (bigger), **nalaklaka** (cheaper). **Dakdakkel ti balayda ngem ti balaymi.** (**ngem** = than)
hint: The same doubling as ongoing verbs.

q: How do you say "Please" and "Nice to meet you"?
a: **Pangngaasim** / **Pangngaasiyo** (please, to one / politely), and **Naragsakak a maam-ammoka** (nice to meet you).

q: Ask "How do I get to the market?"
a: **Kasano ti mapan idiay tiendaan?**

q: What do **Dumiretsoka**, **Kumannigidka** and **Kumannawanka** mean?
a: Go straight ahead, turn left, turn right. Each is an **-um-** verb used as a command with **-ka**.

q: How do you stop a jeepney to get off?
a: **Para!** (friendlier: **Para, manong!**), and **Ditoy laeng** = just here.

q: Ask "How much is the fare to Vigan?"
a: **Manu ti plete inggana idiay Vigan?** (*plete* = fare, *inggana* = until/up to)

q: What does **Alaekon** mean, and how is it built?
a: "I'll take it (now)." **alaen** (take it) + **-k** fused to **-ek** + **-on** (now).

q: Shopping: say "One more", "I'm done" and "I don't want it".
a: **Maysa pay.** (one more: *maysa* = one, *pay* = still, more) · **Nalpasakon.** (I'm done now: **-ak** = I, **-on** = now) · **Diak kayat.** (I don't want it: **di** + *-ko* = **diak**, lesson 9).
hint: Each one reuses a piece you know: pay, -ak + -on, diak.

q: At a carinderia: ask what they have, order something, and ask the total.
a: **Ania ti adda?** (what is there?) · **Kayatko ti ___.** (I'd like ___) · **Mano amin?** (how much altogether?: *mano* = how much, *amin* = all). Pointing at a pot and saying **Daytoy** (this one) works too.

q: Say "Help!", "Look out!" and "I'm lost".
a: **Tulong!** · **Agannadka!** · **Naiyaw-awanak.**

q: Say "I'm sick" and "I need a doctor".
a: **Agsakitak.** and **Masapulko ti doktor.**

q: How do you say "My head hurts"?
a: **Agsakit ti ulok.** The pattern **Agsakit ti ___ + my** works for any body part. "My" follows the -ko rule: **-k** after a vowel (*ulok*), **-ko** after a consonant (*tianko*).

q: Say "My tooth hurts" and "My stomach hurts". Why does one end in -ko?
a: **Agsakit ti ngipenko.** · **Agsakit ti tianko.** Both *ngipen* (tooth) and *tian* (belly, stomach) end in a consonant, so "my" stays whole as **-ko**. After a vowel it shrinks to **-k**: **Agsakit ti matak** (my eye hurts).
hint: Lesson 3: -ko after a consonant, -k after a vowel.

q: How do you say "Take care" and the formal "Goodbye"?
a: **Agaluadka** (to one; **Agaluadkayo** to several or politely) and **Agpakadaakon** ("I'm taking my leave now").
